new_statements.quote: Seperti dalam bahasa Indonesia, tekanan biasanya jatuh pada suku kedua dari akhir kata. Penambahan klitik seperti -pa, -do, -mo, -ki, -a', -ko, atau -ii pada akhir kata tidak merubah penempatan tekanan. Contoh ( ´ menunjukkan tekanan): kaléba 'bangun', kalébado 'sudah bangun'; mampakanánang 'memasak', mampakanánanga' 'saya memasak'; tetapi: sápo 'rumah', sapóna 'rumahnya'.
new_statements.translation: As in Indonesian, stress usually falls on the second syllable from the end of the word. Adding clitics such as -pa, -do, -mo, -ki, -a', -ko, or -ii to the end of a word does not change the placement of stress. Examples (´ marks stress): kaléba 'get up', kalébado 'already got up'; mampakanánang 'cook', mampakanánanga' 'I cook'; but: sápo 'house', sapóna 'his/her house'.
new_statements.citation: Abas, Husen & Ian W. Vail (eds). 1991. Caka-caka' basa To Mamunyu: Percakapan bahasa Mamuju: Mamuju conversations. new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; the stress domain includes true suffixes (e.g. possessive -na: sápo > sapóna) but excludes the enclitics (-pa, -do, -mo, -ki, -a', -ko, -ii), which attach outside the stressed word without shifting stress. Strømme 1994:103 independently states that person clitics 'do not alter the stress of the root word they are attached to, as true suffixes do in Mamuju'.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; hedged with 'biasanya' (usually). Long consonants from clitic attachment (tarrusa' > tarrussa', p. xiii) are described but not tied to stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (root + suffixes), clitics excluded; stated in an orthography guide for a triglot conversation book in the main (prestige) Mamuju dialect ('dialek utama bahasa Mamuju', p. x), written by the SIL team (Strømme) after 1987-1991 fieldwork. Not a phonological monograph.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement describes the main (prestige) Mamuju dialect of Kabupaten Mamuju ('dialek utama bahasa Mamuju', Abas & Vail 1991: x) = Glottolog dialect nucl1567 'Nuclear Mamuju' under mamu1255; Strømme 1994 (same SIL team, 1987-1992 fieldwork in Mamuju, Kalukku, Budong-Budong) is the same variety. Grimes & Grimes 1987 also cover Sumare, Sinyonyoi, Padang, Tappalang and Botteng lists. The earlier scan's 'Smith 1993' is a Proto-Pitu Ulunna Salu reconstruction, not a Mamuju source.

sources.note: Orthography/pronunciation notes in the Pendahuluan (pp. x-xiv): stress usually falls on the second syllable from the end of the word, as in Indonesian; enclitics -pa, -do, -mo, -ki, -a', -ko, -ii do not move it (kaléba/kalébado, mampakanánang/mampakanánanga'), but the suffix -na does (sápo/sapóna). Main (prestige) Mamuju dialect.

sources.note: Appendix E symbols, p. 93: 'Stress in South Sulawesi languages usually occurs on the penultimate syllable. In such cases it is not marked in the word lists.' Six Mamuju-dialect wordlists (MMJ, SNY, SUM, PDG, TAP, BOT) are in the appendix; the Mamuju-specific phonetic note (p. 96) concerns only h/w/r. Group-level survey remark, not a Mamuju description.
